toc.title: 6.1 Strange Food from Around the World
6.2 You Inspire Others by Learning, Not by Teaching
6.4 Grammar II: The present continuous and time expressions
6.5 Writing I: A recipe and a process
Group D: Long writing and model answers

html:
Food is more than fuel: it is memory, culture and sometimes courage. This unit takes you on a tour of the world's strangest dishes, then to the story of a Nepali boy who became a celebrated chef in Britain.

In grammar you will study how to give reasons and purposes and how to use the present continuous; in writing you will write a recipe and an opinion paragraph.

Key learning objectives

Reading: matching words, idioms and meanings; completing sentences from the text; true/false/not given; short answers.

Grammar: connectives of reason and purpose (because, as, since, so that, in order to), present continuous with time expressions. Writing: a recipe or process, and an argument paragraph (To what extent do you agree?).

6.1 Strange Food from Around the World

About the text

"Strange Food from Around the World" is an informal, personal essay about eating unusual dishes while travelling.

The writer begins with a general idea — food can be an adventure and even a challenge — and then gives examples country by country, mixing description with personal reactions ("delicious", "disappointing", "too much").

It uses a friendly, conversational voice, short opinions and an idiom, a bridge too far.

What the text says

Travel gives us the chance to try foods we would never think of eating at home, and for some people eating something unfamiliar is a kind of challenge: you take a risk, and if you enjoy the food you feel you have won. The writer then describes a number of dishes.

Dish Country / region What it is The writer's view
Haggis Scotland The parts of a sheep that people usually do not want — heart, liver and lungs — ground up, mixed with mutton fat, oatmeal and spices, packed in a sheep's stomach and boiled for a few hours A traditional dish; surprising ingredients, but tasty
Shiokara Japan Raw squid mixed with salted, fermented squid guts Strong, salty; you may begin to like it once you are used to it, especially when eating with friends
Bush food (witchetty grubs, bush plants) Australia Foods from the "bush": large wood-eating larvae, native plants Nutty-tasting; can be enjoyed in Australia
Fermented horse milk Central Asia (Mongolia, Kazakhstan) Milk from mares that has fermented into a sour, slightly alcoholic drink The writer was disappointed; it was really bad
Jellyfish China A sea animal that scares many people, turned into a crunchy dish Eaten in China as a normal dish
Snails (escargots) France Served as a main dish, fried or baked with plenty of garlic and butter Very tasty
Bún riêu Vietnam A noodle soup made with crab A well-liked noodle dish
Large insects Many countries Fried or roasted insects The writer finds the larger ones hard because they cannot be eaten in one bite

Vocabulary

Word Meaning Example
ferment to go through a chemical change (often into alcohol or acid) Yoghurt and gundruk are fermented foods.
squid a sea creature with a long soft body, eight arms and two tentacles Fried squid is popular on the coast.
witchetty a large whitish larva that eats wood (an Australian bush food) Aboriginal people eat witchetty grubs.
myrtle a bush with shiny leaves, pink or white flowers, blue-black berries Myrtle berries have a spicy taste.
congeal to change from a fluid to a solid state The fat congealed in the cold.
nutty tasting like nuts The bread has a nutty flavour.

Idioms (the text uses a bridge too far: something that goes beyond what is acceptable):

Idiom Meaning
get out of hand to become difficult to control
miss the boat to be too late to get what you want
break the ice to say or do something to make people feel comfortable
cry over spilt milk to worry over past events that cannot be changed
look before you leap to think about the possible bad results before acting

Themes

  • Food as challenge and adventure. Trying a strange dish is a small act of courage.
  • Culture decides taste. What disgusts one person is a delicacy to another — jellyfish in China, snails in France.
  • Opinion and honesty. The writer is honest even when the food is "really bad".

Questions and model answers

Objective questions (1 mark each)

  1. Haggis is made from the parts of a [1]acowbsheepcpigdfish
  2. Snails are served as a main dish in [1]aJapanbFrancecChinadAustralia
  3. "Ferment" means [1]ato cook in oilbto go through a chemical changecto freezedto dry
  4. Bún riêu is a [1]aVietnamese crab noodle soupbScottish puddingcJapanese rice cakedFrench cheese
Answers

1. (b).

2. (b).

3. (b).

4. (a).

Short-answer questions (2 marks each)

  1. Why does food become a challenge for people when they travel? [2]
  2. How is haggis prepared? [2]
  3. When do you start to like shiokara? [2]
  4. Where can people enjoy bush food? [2]
  5. Why does the writer find it difficult to eat larger insects? [2]
Model answers

1. Because they meet unfamiliar dishes and must decide whether to take the risk of eating them; liking the food feels like a small victory.

2. The heart, liver and lungs of a sheep are ground up and mixed with mutton fat, oatmeal and spices, packed into a sheep's stomach and boiled for a few hours.

3. We start to like it when we have become used to its strong taste, especially while eating it with friends.

4. In Australia.

5. Large insects cannot be eaten in one bite, so the writer has to chew them in several bites, which is harder.

Long-answer questions (4 marks each)

  1. Which of the dishes in the text is the strangest to you? Give reasons. [4]
  2. Write about a traditional Nepali food that a foreigner might find strange. [4]
Model answers

1. To me the strangest dish is shiokara, because it is made of raw squid mixed with the salty, fermented guts of the squid. The idea of eating raw sea animal with its fermented insides is unpleasant to me, and the writer also says the taste is strong. I think a person would need a lot of courage and practice to enjoy it.

2. Gundruk and sinki are fermented leaves and radish that many Nepalis love, yet foreigners may find the smell strange. Another example is kinema, soya beans fermented until they become sticky and strong-smelling, eaten by Limbus and Rais with rice. Sukuti (dried meat) or chhoyela (spiced grilled buffalo meat) may also surprise visitors. For Nepalis these are healthy, traditional foods that remind us of home.

6.2 You Inspire Others by Learning, Not by Teaching

About the text

This text is an interview with Santosh Shah, a chef born in Nepal who works in the United Kingdom and became widely known when he took part in MasterChef: The Professionals (2020) on BBC One.

The title is his philosophy: a person inspires others not by lecturing but by never stopping learning. An interview is a question-and-answer text; its voice is spoken, direct and personal.

What the text says

  • A humble start. Shah comes from a poor family. He did not have a normal childhood; he started working while still a boy, at about nine or ten, to support his family.
  • From the kitchen floor to the top. He began in the lowest jobs in restaurant kitchens, learned by watching and practising, and rose step by step. He worked at the London restaurant Cinnamon Kitchen, and is very proud of what he learned there. He did not receive special favours; he took every task and asked for more.
  • MasterChef. Appearing on the TV show raised his popularity.
  • Experimenting with Nepali food. He wants to show the world that Nepali cuisine is unique and rich and not just "a copy of Indian food". He uses classic ideas with Nepali flavours — for example, he experimented with sukuti (dried meat), dehydrating it for different times to make it soft without losing its taste, and he cooked octopus in Nepali style.
  • Philosophy. Two things make a person successful: asking "what is next?" and refusing to settle in a comfortable position; and continuous learning. He believes in learning from everyone, even junior staff.
  • Dream. He hopes his restaurant Ayla will win a Michelin star, which, he believes, would raise the profile of Nepali food worldwide. He is hopeful about the Nepali food market because food trends are always changing.

Vocabulary

Word Meaning Example
tandoori cooked in a cylindrical clay oven (tandoor) Tandoori chicken is a popular dish.
executive (chef) a person with power to manage an organisation The executive chef plans the menu.
skewer a long pin for holding meat while roasting Chicken was grilled on skewers.
entirety the whole of something He read the book in its entirety.
nostalgia a mixture of pleasure and sadness when remembering the past The smell of dal bhat filled him with nostalgia.
elevate to raise to a more important level The chef wants to elevate Nepali food.
dehydrate to remove water from food to preserve it Sukuti is meat that has been dehydrated.

Themes

  • Humility and learning. Teaching impresses people only if the teacher is still a student.
  • Perseverance. Shah rose through struggle and hard work, not privilege.
  • Pride in identity. He wants Nepali food to be recognised on its own terms.
  • Innovation and tradition together. New techniques (dehydrating, plating) with old flavours.

Questions and model answers

Objective questions (1 mark each)

  1. Write True, False or Not Given: The interview was taken in Nepal. [1]
  2. Write True, False or Not Given: Santosh Shah came from a well-to-do family. [1]
  3. Write True, False or Not Given: Shah is hopeful about the Nepali food market. [1]
  4. "Elevate" means [1]ato lowerbto raise to a higher levelcto cookdto share
Answers

1. False.

2. False — he came from a humble background.

3. True.

4. (b).

Short-answer questions (2 marks each)

  1. What heightened the popularity of Chef Shah? [2]
  2. Did Shah have a normal childhood? Why? [2]
  3. What does Shah want to show the world about Nepali food? [2]
  4. Write two things that Shah was careful about while experimenting with sukuti. [2]
  5. According to Shah, what two things make a person successful? [2]
  6. Why does Shah want a Michelin star for Ayla? [2]
Model answers

1. His participation in MasterChef: The Professionals (2020) on BBC One raised his popularity.

2. No. He came from a poor family and had to start working at about nine or ten years of age to support them.

3. He wants to show that Nepali cuisine is unique, rich and varied, not merely a copy of Indian food.

4. He wanted to make the meat soft but keep its original taste, and he tried drying it for different lengths of time.

5. Always asking "what is next?" and a belief in continuous learning (never settling in a comfort zone).

6. He believes it would raise the profile of Nepali food around the world.

Long-answer question (4 marks)

  1. What have you learnt from the life story of Santosh Shah? [4]
Model answer

1. I have learnt that success comes from hard work and a willingness to learn, not from a rich background.

Santosh Shah was poor and started work as a child, but he kept asking "What is next?" and learned from every kitchen he worked in.

I learnt that one should be proud of one's own culture and show it to the world with confidence, as he does with Nepali food. Finally, I learnt that a person inspires others more by learning humbly than by simply teaching.

6.3 Grammar I: Reasons and purposes

Connectives link ideas. Reason connectives answer Why did it happen?; purpose connectives answer What for?

Meaning Connectives Pattern Example
reason because because + clause I bought a raincoat because the monsoon started.
reason as, since as/since + clause (usually at the start; known reason) As I am stuck in traffic, I won't reach school on time.
reason because of, due to + noun / noun phrase The flight was delayed because of the bad weather.
purpose to to + base verb The city planted trees to reduce traffic noise.
purpose in order to, so as to + base verb (more formal) We queued in order to buy tickets.
purpose so that so that + clause (often with can/could/will/would) We put a table in the room so that Samip can study in private.
result so clause, so clause It rained, so we stayed home.
Common mistakes

Do not use because and so in the same sentence (Because it rained, so we stayed is wrong). Do not write because of + clause (because of it rained). Use so that before a full clause and to before a verb: He works hard so that he can pass / to pass.

Worked example

Problem. Join the sentences with the connective given: "He ran fast. He wanted to catch the bus." (to)

Solution. He ran fast to catch the bus.

Worked example

Problem. Fill in: "The flight was delayed ____ the bad weather." (because / because of)

Solution. A noun phrase follows → because of. The flight was delayed because of the bad weather.

Exercise A — Match the halves

(a) I bought a raincoat and an umbrella (b) I won't be able to get to school on time (c) The construction company has deployed more workers (d) The flight had been delayed (e) The metropolitan city has planted trees at the roadside (f) We have put a table and chair in the spare bedroom

(i) as I am stuck in traffic. (ii) because of the bad weather. (iii) because the monsoon started. (iv) so that they can complete the construction in time. (v) to reduce traffic noise. (vi) so that Samip can study in private.

Key to Exercise A

(a)–(iii), (b)–(i), (c)–(iv), (d)–(ii), (e)–(v), (f)–(vi).

Exercise B — Choose the correct connective

  1. The fair closed early (because / so) the lights were failing.
  2. They stopped the machine (because of / so that) nobody could be hurt.
  3. She studies hard (to / because) get a scholarship.
  4. (As / Although) it was raining, we took umbrellas.
  5. We left early (because / because of) the traffic.
  6. He saved money (so that / since) he could buy a bicycle.
Key to Exercise B

1. because.

2. so that.

3. to.

4. As.

5. because of.

6. so that.

6.4 Grammar II: The present continuous and time expressions

Form: am/is/are + verb-ing. Uses:

Use Time expressions Example
an action happening now now, at the moment, right now, currently, still The boys are playing cricket now.
an action around now (temporary, not exactly this moment) this week, this month, these days, nowadays The local governments are announcing their policies this month.
a planned future action tonight, tomorrow, later today, next week, on Wednesday We're meeting Nabina later today.
a developing change getting, becoming, growing Prices are rising.

Time words such as yesterday, last week, usually, sometimes do not go with the present continuous.

Worked example

Problem. Choose: "What are you doing (this / last) afternoon?"

Solution. The present continuous looks ahead to a plan. this afternoon.

Worked example

Problem. NOW, AROUND or FUTURE? "I'm sorry, I don't have time. I'm attending a meeting."

Solution. Happening at this moment → NOW.

Exercise C — Choose the correct time expression

  1. The boys are playing cricket (already / now).
  2. The doctors are preparing a report (last / this) week.
  3. The students are preparing for a test (at the moment / usually).
  4. (Currently / Sometimes) the economists are working on the country's financial crisis.
  5. The guard is ringing the bell (now / soon). It is time to go!
  6. She is (still / yet) mowing the lawn.
Key to Exercise C

1. now.

2. this.

3. at the moment.

4. Currently.

5. now.

6. still.

Exercise D — Write NOW, AROUND or FUTURE

  1. The local governments are announcing their policies this month.
  2. I think Mr Rai is taking class at the moment.
  3. We're meeting Nabina later today.
  4. We're organising a programme on Wednesday.
  5. They are coming home right now.
  6. Mum is making dinner for us tonight.
Key to Exercise D

1. AROUND.

2. NOW.

3. FUTURE.

4. FUTURE.

5. NOW.

6. FUTURE.

6.5 Writing I: A recipe and a process

A recipe has a title, a list of ingredients with quantities, and method steps in order. Use imperatives and sequence words (first, then, next, after that, finally) and give times (for seven minutes).

Model recipe — Gajar ka halwa (carrot pudding)

Ingredients: 1 kg grated carrots, 1 litre milk, 200 g sugar, 4 green cardamoms (powdered), 3 tablespoons ghee.

Method:

  1. Switch on the stove and melt the ghee in a pan.
  2. Add the grated carrots and fry for about seven minutes until slightly golden brown.
  3. Pour in the milk and stir.
  4. Cook until all the milk has dried up (about twenty minutes).
  5. Add the sugar and cardamom powder and cook for four more minutes.
  6. Turn off the stove. The halwa is ready to serve.
Model recipe — Vegetable momo

Ingredients: 2 cups flour, a little water and salt; for the filling: 2 cups finely chopped cabbage, 1 chopped onion, 1 carrot (grated), 1 teaspoon ginger-garlic paste, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, salt, 1 tablespoon oil.

Method:

  1. Knead the flour with water and salt into a soft dough and rest it for twenty minutes.
  2. Mix all the filling ingredients well.
  3. Roll the dough into thin small circles.
  4. Put one spoon of filling in the centre of each circle and fold into a half-moon or round shape, sealing the edges.
  5. Grease a steamer and arrange the momos in it.
  6. Steam for 10 to 15 minutes. Serve hot with tomato achar.

6.6 Writing II: An opinion paragraph

When asked To what extent do you agree or disagree?, state your position clearly, give two or three reasons with examples, mention the other side briefly, and end with a firm conclusion. Connectives: firstly, moreover, however, therefore, in conclusion.

Task. Many Nepalis now prefer fast food such as noodles, pizza and burgers to typical Nepali food. This harms their health. To what extent do you agree?

Model answer

I largely agree that the growing taste for fast food is harming the health of Nepalis.

Firstly, fast food contains a great deal of oil, salt, sugar and refined flour but very little fibre or protein, so people who eat it often gain weight and are more likely to suffer from diabetes and heart disease.

Moreover, children who fill up on noodles and fizzy drinks may not eat the vegetables, pulses and grains that they need. Traditional meals such as dal, bhat, tarkari and achar are balanced and fresh.

However, fast food is not bad when eaten occasionally, and some Nepali foods, such as deep-fried snacks, are also unhealthy. Therefore, the problem lies in eating too much of it rather than in the food itself.

In conclusion, we should enjoy fast food rarely and make home-cooked Nepali meals our main diet.

Chapter summary

  • Strange Food from Around the World describes haggis (Scotland), shiokara (Japan), bush food (Australia), fermented horse milk, jellyfish (China), snails (France), bún riêu (Vietnam) and large insects; food is an adventure and taste is cultural.
  • Idiom: a bridge too far — too extreme.
  • You Inspire Others by Learning, Not by Teaching is an interview with Nepali chef Santosh Shah (MasterChef: The Professionals 2020, BBC One): humble start, hard work, pride in Nepali food, ambition for a Michelin star for Ayla.
  • Reasons: because, as, since + clause; because of, due to + noun. Purposes: to, in order to, so that.
  • Present continuous: now (now, at the moment), around now (this week, these days) and planned future (tonight, tomorrow, next week).
  • A recipe lists ingredients and numbered steps; an opinion paragraph states a view, gives reasons and concludes.

Practice questions

Objective questions (1 mark each)

  1. "Cry over spilt milk" means [1]aspill milkbworry about things that cannot be changedcdrink milkdbe thirsty
  2. He took a map ____ he would not lose the way. [1]aso thatbbecause ofcalthoughdunless
  3. "We are meeting the principal tomorrow." Here the present continuous shows [1]aa habitba planned future actionca past eventda general truth
  4. Santosh Shah wants a Michelin star for [1]aCinnamon KitchenbAylacMasterChefdBBC One
Answers

1. (b).

2. (a).

3. (b).

4. (b).

Short answer questions (2 marks each)

  1. Why did the writer feel disappointed with the fermented horse milk? [2]
  2. What is Shah's advice for success? [2]
  3. Join using so that: "She switched on the light. She wanted to read." [2]
  4. Complete: "The match was cancelled ____ heavy rain." (because / because of) [2]
Answers

1. Because the drink tasted really bad to the writer.

2. Keep asking "What is next?", never settle in comfort, and keep learning.

3. She switched on the light so that she could read.

4. because of.

Long answer questions (4 marks each)

  1. Write a recipe for dal bhat or sel roti with ingredients and method. [4]
  2. "Fast food is better than home-cooked food." Do you agree? Write a paragraph. [4]
Answers

1. Outline: title; ingredients with quantities; numbered steps with sequence words and times; serving suggestion.

2. Outline: disagree; reasons — nutrition, cost, hygiene; admit that fast food is convenient; conclusion.

Group D: Long writing and model answers

Group D — Extended answers (10 marks each, for deeper revision)

  1. Write a recipe and an opinion paragraph on traditional food. [10]
  2. Explain connectives of reason and purpose and the three uses of the present continuous. [10]

Model answer D1: a recipe and an opinion paragraph (10 marks)

Introduction. A recipe has a title, a list of ingredients with quantities and numbered steps with imperative verbs. An opinion paragraph states a view, gives reasons and concludes.

Model recipe: Sel roti (a Nepali festival bread).

Recipe

Ingredients: 2 cups rice flour, half a cup sugar, 1 ripe banana, 2 spoons ghee, one cup water, oil for frying.
Method:

  1. Mix the flour, sugar and mashed banana in a bowl.
  2. Add the ghee and water slowly and make a smooth, thick batter.
  3. Rest the batter for 30 minutes.
  4. Heat the oil in a deep pan.
  5. Pour the batter in a circle through a funnel into the hot oil.
  6. Fry until golden on both sides, then take it out and serve warm.
    Serves: 4 people.

Model opinion paragraph.

Opinion paragraph

In my opinion, traditional food is better than fast food. Firstly, our dal, bhat and tarkari is full of protein, fibre and vitamins, whereas burgers contain much oil and salt.

Secondly, local food is cheaper because it uses vegetables from our own farms. Thirdly, eating traditional food keeps our culture alive. Some people argue that fast food is quicker and tastier, but quick food can make us unhealthy.

Therefore, I believe we should eat traditional food every day and fast food only rarely.

Points (8).

  1. Title.
  2. Ingredients with exact quantities.
  3. Numbered steps.
  4. Imperatives.
  5. Time and temperature.
  6. Number of servings.
  7. Opinion: topic sentence.
  8. Reasons, counter-argument and conclusion.

Conclusion. Exact quantities and a clear order are needed for a recipe.

Model answer D2: reasons, purposes and the present continuous (10 marks)

Reasons and purposes.

  1. because / as / since + clause: We eat momo because it is tasty.
  2. because of / due to + noun: The shop closed because of the strike.
  3. to / in order to + base verb: She went to the market to buy vegetables.
  4. so that + clause: He saved money so that he could open a restaurant.
  5. so ... that and such ... that show result: The soup was so hot that I could not drink it.

Present continuous (am/is/are + -ing).

  1. Now: The chef is cooking dal at the moment.
  2. Around now: She is learning to cook these days.
  3. Planned future: We are having a feast tomorrow.
Use Time words Example
Now now, at the moment Santosh is tasting the sauce.
Around now this week, these days He is preparing for the competition.
Future plan tonight, next week They are opening a restaurant next month.

Note. State verbs such as know, like, want are not normally used in the continuous: say I like momo, not I am liking momo.

Conclusion. Choose the connective by the grammar that follows it: clause, noun or verb.
